A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preference-divergence data-selection work. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, terminology and organization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama alignment experiments on UltraFeedback, including conflict-level comparisons, selection-budget studies, ablations and detailed benchmark scores in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds HelpSteer, Qwen2.5, Taobao Live and sensitivity experiments, reported in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains cross-aspect proxy reward estimation, quantile normalization, length-balanced sampling, the length penalty, selection of the most negative PD values and subsequent DPO training. DMPO is renamed DFPO, and Algorithm 1 moves into Appendix B; these do not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's UltraFeedback experiments, v2 adds HelpSteer with five preference aspects, UltraChat for Qwen supervised fine-tuning, and a proprietary Taobao Live task generating product-specific sales scripts. The original conflict scenarios, five public evaluation sets and AlpacaEval 2 remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds PD (rati.), which selects using ground-truth discrete aspect ratings, to the reported comparisons. Other apparent additions are matched renamings: RAF corresponds to A1, PD (nl) to A2, OVA. to Overall, and AVG. to Oracle. HIGH and MID remain as PD (high) and PD (mid).

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen2.5-7B policy experiments, additional proxy-model configurations, a 50% main selection budget for HelpSteer, and Taobao evaluations against the SFT model. The reported DPO learning rate changes from 5e-7 in v1 Appendix B.3 to 1e-6 in v2 Appendix C.5; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. The existing public evaluation judges and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity studies of proxy-model size, family and training-data fraction in Figure 5, plus length-penalty and quantile-normalization sweeps in Tables C.3–C.5. Existing conflict, selection-budget, reward-prediction and length-distribution analyses are substantially retained under renamed methods. The former generated-response-length ablation table is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same mean-plus/minus presentation for average win scores. Neither supplies new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures. Changed plus/minus values and additional rows are result changes, not changes in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive HelpSteer, Qwen, Taobao and sensitivity results. Retained UltraFeedback entries also change: OURS at 10% conflict and 30% selection changes from AW 1.26 to 1.24, while A2/PD (nl) at 30% conflict and 50% selection changes from 1.29 to 1.21 (v1 Tables B.3/B.1; v2 Tables E.6/E.8). Generated-response-length results and detailed 10% selection rows are removed. The revised learning-rate disclosure prevents interpreting these revisions as established same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: The loss-bound theorems, selection condition and supporting lemmas remain substantively the same. However, v2 Appendix A.1.1 adds an inconsistent identity: Equation 36 defines the loss as negative expected preference probability, before Equation 37 uses negative expected log probability. v1 Equation 39 directly gives the log-probability loss. The expanded derivation otherwise mainly adds explanation.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains theoretically motivated PD selection for efficient alignment. v2 replaces the abstract's specific claim of over 10% relative improvement against holistic and oracle preferences with a nonquantified claim of consistent improvement over full-data alignment using as little as 30% of the data.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets conflicts as primarily data-quality problems among compatible criteria, qualifying v1's broader discussion of quality trade-offs. It adds explanations of the rating comparator's discretization and annotation costs, proxy-model sensitivity, and why filtering can help even with consistent labels. Appendix D substantially expands limitations concerning reward-model dependence, distribution shift and the offline setting, alongside possible iterative, alternative-objective and distillation extensions.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset counts, Qwen's SFT-data assignment, HelpSteer reward prompts and Taobao annotation details while retaining most of the training recipe. It revises the DPO learning rate and removes the explicit count of 16 H20 GPUs. A new statement claims supplementary processing/training code, whose availability cannot be verified from the PDFs; its assertion that all datasets are public conflicts with the proprietary Taobao experiment.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for UltraChat, scaling laws, HelpSteer and HelpSteer2, and removes the Stiennon and Ziegler references. Related work expands the discussion of alignment-data quality versus pre-training scale, while retaining the central positioning against single-preference filtering and multi-objective alignment.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, terminology is revised throughout, and the experimental narrative is reorganized into six result subsections. Detailed setup and the algorithm move into appendices, while the derivation receives a four-step explanatory structure. These are substantial editorial and organizational changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting. Main comparison tables are rebuilt, budget plots are reorganized, the ablation table is replaced by plots, and new sensitivity and downstream-result displays are added. Detailed appendix tables are restructured, while the existing heatmaps and distribution figures are largely retained.

improvement.justification: HelpSteer and Qwen experiments substantially address v1's reliance on one preference dataset and one policy-model family. Proxy-model and hyperparameter sensitivity tests also strengthen support for the method's practical reliability, and the expanded limitations clarify its scope. These gains outweigh localized reporting defects, including the new missing-log identity, inconsistent Qwen AW summaries between Tables C.2 and E.10, and the public-data claim contradicting the proprietary experiment.
